overview: The Golden Horde grew from the western conquests of the Mongol Empire and became a major power connecting the Eurasian steppe, Rus principalities and trading cities. Its history includes skilled metalwork, multilingual books, mobile households and ambitious urban building. The later Great Horde appears under the map’s 1492 label. The dated examples below distinguish fourteenth-century daily life from the politics of the late fifteenth century.

periods.title: Conquest and the Jochid inheritance
periods.summary: Batu’s campaigns established a western dominion ruled by descendants of Jochi, Genghis Khan’s eldest son. Conquest placed existing communities under new rulers.

periods.title: An independent Eurasian power
periods.summary: The Golden Horde emerged as an independent power in the 1260s. Trade, diplomacy and religious connections linked its steppe and urban communities with neighboring states.

periods.title: Civil war and changing alliances
periods.summary: Rival khans contested power. Tokhtamysh briefly reunited major Jochid territories, then fought his former supporter Timur; fragmentation followed.

periods.title: The Great Horde and rival successors
periods.summary: The Great Horde claimed seniority among competing successors. Its defeat in 1502 transferred power without ending Jochid traditions.

items.text: Batu’s forces conquered the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas in 1236-1240. His dynasty descended from Jochi. The map’s first appearance in 1279 therefore comes decades after its rise.
Berke was Muslim, and all khans from Öz Beg onward followed Islam. An alliance with Egypt’s Mamluk rulers in 1262-1263 also shows how diplomacy reached far beyond the steppe.

Bolgar preserves a mosque, minaret, mausoleums, baths and palace remains. These buildings make urban life visible alongside the better-known horse-riding armies. Its history also joins nomadic communities to settled craft and trading centers.

At Kitsivka 1 in present-day Ukraine, archaeologists found pottery, metal vessels, tools and clothing fittings from the Golden Horde period. The settlement stood near a river crossing. Such finds reveal everyday work and connections, rather than just the names of rulers.

A steel helmet decorated with silver may bear Jani Beg’s name. The Metropolitan Museum treats that reading as a possibility, not a certainty. The object still shows skilled metalworking and the use of inscriptions on prestigious equipment.

A silver half-dirham of Tokhtamysh in Oxford is only 18 millimeters across. Its mint name, royal titles and religious words fit on that small surface. Coins could carry both money value and a ruler’s public message.

sections.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s

items.text: Ibn Battuta described felt-covered homes carried on wagons, with horses, oxen or camels pulling them. Moving house could mean taking the house along. His account describes travelers and a royal camp, not every household.
He recorded millet porridge with mare’s milk, meat and pasta cooked with milk. These are a visitor’s observations, not a menu shared by everyone across an enormous territory.

Elite wives and princesses could control property and exercise authority. Court households also depended on servants and enslaved people. A queen’s influence tells us little about the freedoms of the women serving her.

Black Sea markets traded grain, furs, wax and honey, alongside goods arriving from farther east. They also sold enslaved people. Commercial connections created wealth, but could bring captivity and family separation.

sections.title: Learning and a small writing sample

items.text: The fourteenth-century Codex Cumanicus contains vocabulary in Latin, Persian and Cuman, a Turkic language. Preserved in Venice, it shows people assembling tools for communication across languages. A word list is a practical achievement: conversations do not translate themselves.

Bolgar’s nomination dossier describes madrasahs, institutions for education, among its fourteenth-century urban developments. These references show organized learning, but do not tell us that every child attended school or had the same opportunities.

An Arabic sample from Tokhtamysh’s late-fourteenth-century coin reads “السلطان الاعظم” (al-sultan al-aʿzam), meaning “the supreme sultan.” It is a royal title, not evidence that all residents spoke Arabic at home. This inscription belongs to the earlier Golden Horde, before the Great Horde’s final decades.

An archaeological study published in 2002 counted 25 excavated Golden Horde bathhouses: 14 communal and 11 private. That was the evidence known to its author then. Baths were substantial urban buildings, with washing also important in Muslim religious life.

Bolgar’s fourteenth-century development included water supply and drainage, according to its heritage dossier. These systems required planning and maintenance. The evidence cited here does not establish what sort of toilet every household used; bathhouses and drains are not proof of a flush toilet in every home.

Medieval writers mention a hospital, or bimaristan, at Urgench. A modern study uses those reports to investigate care in the Golden Horde. Details reconstructed by comparison with other hospitals remain proposals, and the evidence does not establish a hospital in every town.

A study of medieval accounts describes hot and mineral springs used as treatments, as well as bathing. This tells us what people tried when ill. It does not show that those treatments worked by modern medical standards.

Civil war followed Berdibeg’s death in 1359. Tokhtamysh later reunited much of the Jochid realm, but conflict with Timur weakened his position. The larger Golden Horde eventually divided into several states.
By the 1430s, the Great Horde claimed to be the senior continuation of the old realm. Other khanates pursued their own authority.
Ahmed Khan withdrew from the Ugra confrontation in 1480. This weakened his claim over Muscovy, but the Great Horde continued afterward.
In 1501-1502, harsh winter conditions, shortages and desertions undermined Shaikh Ahmed. Politics depended on feeding people and animals as well as winning alliances.
Crimea’s Mengli Giray defeated Shaikh Ahmed in 1502. Shaikh Ahmed survived. The often-repeated story that Sarai was destroyed that year is disputed.

Successor khanates inherited political and literary traditions of the Golden Horde. Its legacy reached across Crimea, Central Asia and Siberia. A political breakup did not make languages, skills or communities disappear.

ending.text: The Great Horde lost power to the Crimean khan in 1502. This was a political defeat within a wider succession of states, not the disappearance of the Golden Horde’s peoples. Jochid political and literary traditions continued in successor khanates.
